{{short description|Informal fallacy that the way one sees the world reflects the way the world really is}}
The '''mind projection fallacy''' is an [[informal fallacy]] that occurs when a person believes in [[Claim (philosophy)|factual claims]] (as distinguished from [[facts]]) solely based on mental or sensory experiences,<ref name="Taliaferro2018">{{cite book | last=Taliaferro | first=Charles | title=Bad Arguments: 100 of the most important fallacies in Western philosophy | chapter=Mind Projection | publisher=Wiley | date=9 May 2018 | isbn=978-1-119-16578-1 | doi=10.1002/9781119165811.ch89 | url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/9781119165811.ch89 | access-date=1 December 2025 | pages=369–370}}</ref> which are often interpreted as objective properties.<ref name="Graham2025"/> That is, someone's subjective judgments are "projected" to be inherent properties of an object, rather than being related to personal perception. One consequence is that others may be assumed to share the same perception, or that they are irrational or misinformed if they do not. The idea has been compared to [[Plato]]'s [[allegory of the cave]].<ref name="Graham2025"/>

For example, it is fallacious to say that [[sweetness]] is an inherent property of [[sugar]] molecules; instead, it results from the human perception of those molecules.<ref name="Taliaferro2018"/><ref name="Graham2025"/> Similarly, a person may dismiss a subject as uninteresting based on their personal lack of interest,<ref name="Taliaferro2018"/> or believe in a [[flat earth]] based on their intuitive perception that the world around them is flat.<ref name="Graham2025"/>

There is also a "negative" form of the fallacy, in which someone assumes that their own lack of knowledge about a phenomenon (a fact about their state of mind) means that the phenomenon is not or cannot be understood (a fact about reality; see also [[Map–territory relation#"The map is not the territory"|Map and territory]]).<ref name="PTAL"/> This form of the fallacy is similar to the [[argument from ignorance]].

==History==
The mind projection fallacy was first described by physicist and [[Bayesian inference|Bayesian]] philosopher [[Edwin Thompson Jaynes|E.&nbsp;T. Jaynes]], who wrote that:<ref name="PTAL"/>
{{quote|[I]n studying probability theory, it was vaguely troubling to see reference to "gaussian random variables", or "stochastic processes", or "stationary time series", or "disorder", as if the property of being gaussian, random, stochastic, stationary, or disorderly is a real property, like the property of possessing mass or length, existing in Nature. Indeed, some seek to develop statistical tests to determine the presence of these properties in their data...<br/>
Once one has grasped the idea, one sees the Mind Projection Fallacy everywhere; what we have been taught as deep wisdom, is stripped of its pretensions and seen to be instead a foolish ''[[Non sequitur (logic)|non sequitur]]''. The error occurs in two complementary forms, which we might indicate thus: (A) (My own imagination) → (Real property of Nature), [or] (B) (My own ignorance) → (Nature is indeterminate)}}

Jaynes described the fallacy as occurring when someone thinks that the way they see the world reflects the way the world really is, going as far as assuming the real existence of imagined objects.<ref name="PTAL">{{cite book |pages=1–16|author= E. T. JAYNES |title=Maximum Entropy and Bayesian Methods |chapter=Probability Theory as Logic |date=1990 |url=http://bayes.wustl.edu/etj/articles/prob.as.logic.pdf |access-date=2011-05-19 |doi=10.1007/978-94-009-0683-9_1|isbn=978-94-010-6792-8}}</ref> He used the example of failing to distinguish between "The room is noisy" and "There is noise in the room"; one statement is [[Ontology|ontological]], describing the nature of reality, and the other is [[Epistemology|epistemological]], describing someone's personal perception.<ref name="Joronen2007">{{cite book | last=Joronen | first=Tero | title=Theoretical Advances and Applications of Fuzzy Logic and Soft Computing | chapter=Perceptions for Making Sense, Description Language for Meaning Articulation | series=Advances in Soft Computing | publisher=Springer Berlin Heidelberg | publication-place=Berlin, Heidelberg | volume=42 | date=2007 | isbn=978-3-540-72433-9 | doi=10.1007/978-3-540-72434-6_14 | chapter-url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/978-3-540-72434-6_14 | access-date=1 December 2025 | pages=128–138}}</ref> 

A 2012 edition of the 1989 conference proceedings where Jaynes described the mind projection fallacy called it a "fundamental contribution to the art and science of thinking".<ref name="Fougere2012">{{cite book | last=Fougère | first=P. F. | title=Maximum Entropy and Bayesian Methods | publisher=Springer Science & Business Media | date=6 December 2012 | isbn=978-94-009-0683-9 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=sLz0CAAAQBAJ | access-date=1 December 2025 | page=viii}}</ref>

==Usage==
Jaynes used the concept to argue against the [[Copenhagen interpretation]] of [[quantum mechanics]].<ref>{{cite book |year=1989 |last1=Jaynes |first1=E. T. |title=Maximum Entropy and Bayesian Methods |chapter=Clearing up Mysteries — the Original Goal |pages=1–27 | url=http://bayes.wustl.edu/etj/articles/cmystery.pdf |doi=10.1007/978-94-015-7860-8_1|isbn=978-90-481-4044-2 }}</ref> He also criticized the idea of [[Uncertainty quantification|aleatory uncertainty]] (inherent randomness), with one author describing the issue as, "our uncertainty is ascribed to an inherent property of nature, or, more generally, our models of reality are confused with reality. From a pragmatic point of view, regardless of one's philosophical position on this issue, all one can say is that there is not sufficient information to make perfect predictions or deductions."<ref name="Beck2010">{{cite journal | last=Beck | first=James L. | title=Bayesian system identification based on probability logic | journal=Structural Control and Health Monitoring | volume=17 | issue=7 | date=2010 | doi=10.1002/stc.424 | pages=825–847 | url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/stc.424 | access-date=1 December 2025| url-access=subscription }}</ref> It has also been used to criticize the concept of [[emergence]]<ref name="Graham2025">{{cite book | last=Graham | first=Liam | title=Physics Fixes All the Facts | publisher=Springer Nature Switzerland | publication-place=Cham | date=2025 | isbn=978-3-031-69287-1 | doi=10.1007/978-3-031-69288-8_4 | url=https://link.springer.com/10.1007/978-3-031-69288-8_4 | access-date=1 December 2025}}</ref> and to discuss the nature of probability in [[Law|legal]] contexts.<ref name="Robertson1993">{{cite journal | last1=Robertson | first1=Bernard | last2=Vignaux | first2=G. A. | title=Probability—The Logic of the Law | journal=Oxford Journal of Legal Studies | volume=13 | issue=4 | date=1993 | issn=0143-6503 | doi=10.1093/ojls/13.4.457 | pages=457–478 | url=https://academic.oup.com/ojls/article-lookup/doi/10.1093/ojls/13.4.457 | access-date=1 December 2025| url-access=subscription }}</ref>

The mind projection fallacy has been described as a common error in [[philosophy]].<ref name="Taliaferro2018"/><ref name="Graham2025"/>

==Cognitive science==
The mind projection fallacy has been described as a potential issue in [[artificial intelligence]] research.<ref name="Sarkadi2019">{{cite book | last1=Sarkadi | first1=Ştefan | last2=Panisson | first2=Alison R. | last3=Bordini | first3=Rafael H. | last4=McBurney | first4=Peter | last5=Parsons | first5=Simon | title=Agreement Technologies | chapter=Towards an Approach for Modelling Uncertain Theory of Mind in Multi-Agent Systems | publisher=Springer International Publishing | publication-place=Cham | volume=11327 | date=2019 | isbn=978-3-030-17293-0 | doi=10.1007/978-3-030-17294-7_1 | chapter-url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/978-3-030-17294-7_1 | access-date=1 December 2025 | page=3–17}}</ref> In addition, the tendency of humans to [[anthropomorphize]] non-human intelligences as having human-like minds has been described a type of mind projection fallacy.<ref name="Yampolskiy2012">{{cite book | last1=Yampolskiy | first1=Roman V. | last2=Fox | first2=Joshua | title=Singularity Hypotheses: A Scientific and Philosophical Assessment | chapter=Artificial General Intelligence and the Human Mental Model | publisher=Springer Berlin Heidelberg | publication-place=Berlin, Heidelberg | date=2012 | isbn=978-3-642-32559-5 | doi=10.1007/978-3-642-32560-1_7 | chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/10.1007/978-3-642-32560-1_7 | access-date=1 December 2025 | pages=129–145}}</ref>
